Data Request 1 (Resource Report 1 – General Project Description):
Northern states typical daytime hours of construction would be from 7:00 AM to 10:00 PM. Indicate if night
work would occur, when nighttime hours would begin, and provide a detailed list of all activities that may
occur during nighttime hours.

Response:
Nighttime hours would begin at 10:00PM. Nighttime construction may include hydrostatic testing,
commissioning, blowdowns, tie-ins, electrical work, inspections, and erosion control installation and
repairs, dewatering, equipment delivery, emergencies, concrete pours, or other atypical circumstances that
are time- and/or temperature-sensitive.

In particular, the HDD crossings may be conducted continuously (i.e., 24 hours per day), including
overnight, at critical times such as during pullback of the pipe into the drill hole on the longer drills and
when pipe sections will need to be welded during pullback. See Section 1.5.1 of Resource Report 1.

Data Request 3 (Resource Report 1 – General Project Description):
Characterize the environmental baseline in the project area by identifying general environmental trends
and physiographic characteristics, how the environment has changed over time, and any environmental
concerns in the project area.

Response:
Environmental baseline conditions in the Project area are characterized by a semi-arid setting shaped by
drought, wind erosion, internal drainage, agricultural conversion, oil and gas development, and localized
habitat fragmentation.

The Project includes two geographic areas. The main Project area is about 3–7 miles west and south of
Hobbs, New Mexico, and is primarily in Lea County, New Mexico, but extends east of the state line into
Gaines County, Texas. The secondary Project area is 4 miles east of Denver City, Texas, in Yoakum
County.

The Project is in the Southern High Plains subregion of the Great Plains, and this setting is an ecological
transition zone between Great Plains grasslands and Southwestern desert scrublands. This is the Llano
Estacado, an expansive semi-arid plateau spanning west Texas and far eastern New Mexico. Ecologically,
the Llano Estacado is where shortgrass prairies of the Plains meets the grasslands of the Chihuahuan
desert.

Historically, the region was predominated by grama grasses and buffalograss with more arid portions of
the plateau on the southwest transitioning to increasing shinnery oak, mesquite, saltbush, and sagebrush.
Annual precipitation ranges from 12–20 inches, decreasing from the northeast to southwest. High
evaporation rates and periodic drought are significant ecological controls, and wind is a dominant
environmental mechanism contributing to erosion and deposition. Fauna on the Llano Estacado are
diverse. Mammals include herbivores like pronghorn and mule deer, carnivores like coyote, bobcat, and
fox, and small mammals like jackrabbits, squirrels, gophers, rats, and mice. Birds include grass and
shrubland species like quail and prairie-chicken, a diversity of raptors, and wetland playa settings can
intermittently support cranes, geese, and ducks. The semi-arid climate hosts a diverse assemblage of
reptiles like snakes, lizards, and turtles.

The bedrock geology of the Llano Estacado reflects episodes of marine sedimentary deposition during the
Paleozoic and Mesozoic Eras. Germain to the Project area, the southern portion of the Llano Estacado
overlies the Permian Basin, a deep structural depression infilled with a sedimentary stratigraphy of
limestone, sandstone, and evaporites. The Permian Basin is an important crude oil and natural gas
producing structure.
                                                                                                 Page 2 of 4

The surface of the basement-rock deposits are a massive unconformity where erosion removed late
Mesozoic and early Cenozoic rocks before the modern configuration of the plateau began to form. This
unconformity is overlain by the Ogallala Formation, a deep unit of clastic sedimentary deposits emplaced
as an apron of alluvial outwash derived from the Rocky Mountains during the Miocene–Pliocene Epochs.
The Ogallala is an important ground water aquifer across much of the Central and Southern Great Plains.

On the Llano Estacado, the Ogallala is intermittently capped by a thick layer of lithified caliche formed by
a long interval of groundwater evaporation and the precipitation of calcium carbonate. Especially to the
east, this cap rock helps define the flat, unbroken terrain of the Llano Estacado plateau. Depending on the
local deposition and preservation, the Ogallala Formation or the caprock can be overlain by younger
alluvial, eolian, and playa deposits laid down during the Pleistocene and Holocene, like the Blackwater
Draw Formation.

The Hobbs Project area, encompassing almost 3,300 acres, is on the southwest margin of the greater
Southern High Plains plateau, and is classified ecologically as the Arid Llano Estacado. In the Hobbs
Project area, surficial geologic deposits are mapped as the Ogallala Formation overlain by a variable
thickness of eolian sands, which are more prominent moving east through the Project area. The local soils
can be generalized as well-drained, loamy to sandy soils that formed in a residuum of weathered
sedimentary rocks and eolian deposits. These tend to be arid but moderately fertile soils where agricultural
productivity can be markedly enhanced with ground water irrigation.

The Hobbs Project area is in the Monument Draw watershed, where an ephemeral stream system is
characterized by discontinuous channels following the Monument Draw Trough, a collapsed structure
formed by the dissolution of the underlying Permian Basin evaporites. Characteristic of the Llano
Estacado, much of the Project area is internally drained by playas, shallow depressions, intermittent
swales, and segments of poorly integrated channels. Run off typically pools and infiltrates alluvial
sediments rather than remaining as surface flow for long distances.

The Denver City Project area, encompassing about 27 acres, lies along the western edge of the Llano
Estacado ecological region. Although units are intermittently preserved, the local generalized Cenozoic
stratigraphy is the Ogallala Formation overlain by the Blackwater Draw formation capped by sheet sands.
The mapped surficial deposits at the Denver City location are Pleistocene-age windblown sands that may
be up to 10 feet thick, and the local soils are well developed loamy fine sands that formed in the older
eolian deposits. These have a moderate agricultural potential for dryland farming, but productivity can be
stabilized and enhanced with irrigation. The Denver City Project area is in the McKenzie Draw watershed,
and this ephemeral channel is about 300–600 feet west of the Project area but does not provide any
potential for overbank alluvial deposition.

Contemporary land use in and around the Hobbs and Denver City Project areas are dominated by two
activities—oil and gas production and agriculture. This is the Permian Basin, a major production area, and
wells, pipelines, processing and ancillary facilities, and their access roads are common features on the
landscape. Oil and gas infrastructure is particularly common in the western quarter of the Hobbs Project
area and surrounding the Denver City locality. There is a long history of agricultural activities in the
region as livestock production and cultivation. The central half of the Hobbs Project area is unbroken
grass-to-scrubland that is suitable for cattle ranching, especially combined with intermittently available
surface water in playas and basins. Row crop agriculture is regionally important, and especially productive
when combined with modern irrigation techniques. The local crops include cotton, peanuts, hay crops, and
                                                                                                Page 3 of 4

grains like sorghum, corn, wheat, and milo. The eastern quarter of the Hobbs Project area and most of the
Denver City Project area are under cultivation.

The Project area is on the periphery of Hobbs, New Mexico, and Denver City, Texas, and outside of oil
and gas infrastructure, development is rare in and immediately around the Project area. The small
residential community of Nadine, isolated to the south of Hobbs, is adjacent to the Hobbs Project area, as
is the Lea County Regional Airport. At the Denver City Project area there is minor dispersed residential
development to the southwest, a natural gas facility to the north, and an electric generation plant to the
northeast. Public infrastructure includes limited road development as U.S. Highway 62, New Mexico State
Highways 8 and 18, and Yoakum County Road 355, with these rights-of-way hosting various utilities.

Native American occupations of the region began during the terminal Pleistocene. The Llano Estacado
evidences early Paleoindian sites, such as Blackwater Draw, Lubbock Lake, Midland, and Plainview.
With the subsequent Archaic period, climatic conditions warmed and dried, which pressured Native
American groups to diversify diets through flexible subsistence strategies and seasonally organized
mobility. Mobile hunter-gatherers of the Archaic exploited wild plant foods and small game, but
economies relied substantially on bison.

The adoption of ceramics and bow-and-arrow technology marks the transition to the Formative period.
Formative populations retained substantial residential mobility and relied primarily on wild plants and
bison, but they increasingly occupied residential sites and supplemented their diets with maize. After
about CE 1450, many residential settlements were abandoned, ceramic production and exchange declined,
and the Native American populations adopted more mobile lifeways centered heavily on bison hunting.

Over time, the Project area has changed from a sparsely settled grassland and shrubland landscape to a
modern ranching, agricultural, and energy-producing landscape. Permanent settlement, livestock grazing,
dryland farming, irrigation technology, mechanized agriculture, transportation improvements, and
intensive oil and gas development altered native vegetation communities, increased surface disturbance,
expanded road and utility corridors, and changed patterns of land use across the Llano Estacado.
Cultural resource investigations were conducted for the Project area and identified 11 cultural resources,
all in Lea County. These include 10 archaeological sites and one railroad documented as a historic cultural
property. Five properties were determined eligible for the National Register of Historic Places, four were
determined not eligible, and two remain unevaluated. Project activities are not proposed at the Register-
eligible properties, and the New Mexico and Texas State Historic Preservation Offices issued findings of
no historic properties affected for the Project.

Existing environmental concerns in the Project area include progressive desertification associated with
climate change, prolonged drought, and declining vegetative cover, which increase the landscape’s
susceptibility to eolian deflation, soil erosion, and the loss of productive topsoil. Additional concerns
include potential land subsidence related to groundwater withdrawal from the Ogallala aquifer and the
dissolution of underlying Permian Basin evaporite deposits. Because much of the region is internally
drained, development, grading, roads, and other surface disturbances can alter sheet flow and disrupt
runoff entering playas, swales, and ephemeral channels. Expanding oil and gas infrastructure, agriculture,
and urban development also contribute to the loss and fragmentation of native grassland, shrubland, and
sandy habitats. These disturbances increase the potential for invasive species to become established and
spread along roads, utility corridors, agricultural margins, and other disturbed areas.
                                                                                               Page 4 of 4

Together, these conditions indicate that the Project area’s environmental baseline is defined by a semi-
arid plateau environment, limited surface-water development, internally drained playas and ephemeral
channels, extensive agricultural and oil and gas land uses, and environmental concerns associated with
drought, erosion, groundwater use, surface disturbance, habitat fragmentation, and invasive species.

Data Request 4 (Resource Report 1 – General Project Description):
Address the comments of the Environmental Protection Agency filed in the Commission’s administrative
record on August 8, 2026.

Response:
Attachment A to this Environmental Information Request provides responses to the Environmental
Protection Agency’s comments filed in the Commission’s administrative record on August 8, 2026.

Posted: 09/23/2026                                                       Responsibility: LD Stephens
                                                                                     Attachment A


EPA’s Comment:

Water Quality

EPA recommends the environmental document describe existing surface, groundwater, and
watershed conditions and assess potential impacts to water quality and quantity, including
impairments. EPA also recommends the environmental document address natural drainage patterns
and potential impacts to floodplains.

Northern’s Response:

Northern Natural Gas Company’s (Northern) Resource Report 2, Sections 2.1 and 2.2 address the
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) recommendations and comments related to
existing conditions of water quality and water resources, as well as proposed mitigation, for the
Permian Expansion Project (Project).

Section 2.1 provides a discussion of groundwater resources such as, sole source aquifers, wells
and springs, wellhead protection areas, and potential sources of groundwater contamination;
however, no sole source aquifers or wellhead protection areas are crossed by the Project. Section
2.1.2 discusses potential impacts and mitigation for wells within 150 feet of construction
workspaces. Sections 2.2.2 and 2.2.4.4 provide discussions of surface waters and potential
impacts; however, no waterbodies are crossed by the Project. Section 2.2.1 and Table 2.2.1-1
provides a discussion of watersheds and river basins crossed by the Project. Section 2.2.4 provides
a discussion of potential water quality and quantity impacts including water use for hydrostatic
testing, trench dewatering, and erosion and sediment controls. Additionally, Resource Report 1,
Table 1.5.3-1 provides estimated quantity and discharge locations for hydrostatic test water.
Section 2.2.2.1 provides a discussion of special status waterbodies; however, no impaired
waterbodies classified under Section 303(d) of the Clean Water Act are crossed by the Project.
Section 2.2.2 also provides a discussion of natural drainage patterns, including arroyos, and
Section 2.2.2.2 provides a discussion on floodplains.
                                                                                      Attachment A


EPA’s Comment:

Water Quality

EPA recommends the environmental document describes any disturbance areas, including an
acreage by land cover (e.g., forest, riparian, floodplains, agricultural, grassland, and
developed/open). Additionally, the environmental document should describe the restoration plan
for restoring the remaining acreage to former uses (e.g., restoration methods, performance
standards, and timeframes). EPA also recommends the environmental document describe the short-
term and long-term impacts of the disturbance areas, including any residual effects and the
mitigation and monitoring measures.

Northern’s Response:

Northern’s Resource Report 3, Section 3.2 and Table 3.2-1, as well as Resource Report 8,
Section 8.1, Table 8.1-1 and Table 8.1-2 provide a discussion of the existing vegetation cover
types and land uses, including potential impacts from construction and operation of the facilities.
Northern will adhere to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s 2013 Upland Erosion
Control, Revegetation, and Maintenance Plan to restore temporary construction workspaces.
Additionally, Sections 8.1.2 and 8.2.1 address restoration in agricultural areas and access roads.
Section 8.2 describes the short-term impacts and mitigation to land uses. Resource Report 1
Section 1.11.7 and Table 1.11-1 describes the cumulative long-term potential impacts.
                                                                                     Attachment A


EPA’s Comment:

National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System

EPA recommends the environmental document evaluate the applicability of Clean Water Act
Section 402 regulations, including 40 CFR §122.26(b)(14)(x) and §122.26(b)(15), to clarify
when National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit coverage is required for
operators of construction activities that discharge stormwater. Clarifying these requirements will
reduce uncertainty for regulated entities, ensure consistent application of permitting obligations,
and strengthen compliance with federal water quality protections by promoting effective
implementation of best management practices.

Northern’s Response:

Northern has evaluated the applicability of Clean Water Act Section 402 regulations, including
those activities defined under 40 CFR §122.26(b)(14)(x) and §122.26(b)(15). The Project
includes constructing an interstate natural gas pipeline, exempting the Project from NPDES
construction stormwater permitting requirements under 40 Code of Federal Regulations
122.26(a)(2)(ii). As shown in Northern’s Resource Report 1, Sections 1.5.3 and 2.0, as well as
Table 1.8-1, Northern has prepared a project-wide Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan
(SWPPP) and will implement the listed best management practices BMPs), as needed, to
minimize discharges of pollutants, including sediment, in stormwater both during and after
construction activities to help ensure protection of surface water quality during storm events.
Appropriate controls would be those suitable to the site conditions and consistent with generally
accepted engineering design criteria and manufacturer specifications. In addition, Federal Energy
Regulatory Commission’s 2013 Upland Erosion Control, Revegetation, and Maintenance Plan
and the Wetland and Waterbody Construction and Mitigation Procedures to mitigate potential
impacts.

In the event of an unforeseen noncompliance or reportable release, Northern will maintain BMPs
as described in the SWPPP and submit a Notice of Intent with the SWPPP to acquire stormwater
coverage. Northern will also obtain coverage under NPDES for hydrostatic test water discharges.
                                                                                      Attachment A


EPA’s Comment:

Clean Water Act Section 303(d)

EPA recommends the environmental document identify any impaired waters under Section
303(d) within the project area, describe applicable TMDLs (e.g., common waterbody name, state
waterbody IDs, segments, and impairments), assess how proposed activities may affect ongoing
restoration or protection efforts, and evaluate mitigation to prevent further degradation. The
environmental document should provide a preliminary inventory of perennial, intermittent, and
ephemeral waterbody crossings by milepost and state and describe proposed crossing methods.
EPA recommends also the environmental document address estimated hydrostatic test water and
trench dewatering volumes and identify potential discharge locations and receiving waters.

Northern’s Response:

Northern’s Resource Report 2, Section 2.2.2.1 identifies that no Clean Water Act 303(d) listed
waters are crossed by the Project. As described above, Resource Report 2, Sections 2.2.2 and
2.2.4.4 provide discussions of surface waters and potential impacts; however, no waterbodies are
crossed by the Project. Resource Report 2, Section 2.2.4.1 and 2.2.4.2 describe water use for
hydrostatic testing and trench dewatering, respectively. Additionally, Resource Report 1, Section
1.11.1 clarifies that water for hydrostatic testing will be from a public water source and
discharged into a well-vegetated upland area adjacent to the ROW or hauled off for disposal at
either a Publicly Owned Treatment Works or Class I or II UIC well. Table 1.5.3-1 provides the
hydrostatic test water segments for the Project with estimated volumes and potential discharge
locations. Trench dewatering is only anticipated after large precipitation events, which makes
volumes estimates infeasible. Since Northern’s initial geotechnical boring data indicates that the
groundwater is significantly lower that the excavated trench, it is unlikely trench dewatering will
be required.
                                                                                    Attachment A


EPA’s Comment:

Coordination with Tribal Governments

If applicable, EPA recommends the environmental document describe the government-to-
government consultation process between the lead agency and affected Tribes, including issues
raised and how they were addressed in selecting the proposed alternative.

Northern’s Response:

Northern’s Resource Report 4, Section 4.5 addresses tribal communities within the Project area
and Table 4.5-1 lists the federally recognized Native American Tribes that were contacted, as
well as the dates of the initial and follow-up notification letters. Only one Tribe, the Tonkawa
Tribe, responded without objection but requested they be notified “if any human remains,
funerary objects, or other evidence of historical or cultural significance is inadvertently
discovered.”
                                                                                      Attachment A


EPA’s Comment:

Biological Resources, Habitat, and Wildlife

EPA recommends the environmental document address the requirements of the Endangered
Species Act including the identification of candidate and listed species, designated critical
habitat and species potentially affected by each alternative, along with practicable mitigation and
the outcome of any consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS). EPA also
recommends that the environmental document describe baseline habitat conditions, anticipated
impacts, and measures for monitoring, adaptive management, and compensatory mitigation,
including potential lands for habitat replacement. EPA further recommends addressing habitat
fragmentation, wildlife movement, and impacts from construction, installation, and maintenance
activities (e.g., trenching, grading, filling, fencing). EPA recommends the environmental
document incorporate any applicable USFWS guidance, supporting data or modeling.

Northern’s Response:

Northern’s Resource Report 3, Section 3.4 provides a discussion of threatened and endangered
species. Section 3.4.2 and Table 3.4.2-1 provide the USFWS Information for Planning and
Consultation list of federally listed threatened, endangered, proposed, and candidate species and
federally designated critical habitat that may be present within the Project area. Existing habitat
conditions, habitat fragmentation, wildlife movement, and impacts from construction,
installation, and maintenance activities are described throughout Sections 3.1, 3.2, and 3.3,
respectively.

As described in Section 3.4.2.6, Northern determined that the Project actions will have no effect
on the federally listed lesser prairie-chicken, piping plover, or rufa red knot. Northern also
determined that Project actions will not jeopardize the continued existence of the experimental,
non-essential populations and species proposed for federal listing: northern aplomado falcon and
monarch butterfly. The New Mexico ESFO and Texas Coastal & Central Plains ESFO responded
to Northern’s request for review and comment and concluded that consultation or conference
under Section 7 of the ESA is not needed. Therefore, consultation is complete.
                                                                                    Attachment A


EPA’s Comment:

Air Quality

EPA recommends that the environmental document provide a detailed assessment of ambient air
conditions, applicable National Ambient Air Quality Standards and non-NAAQS pollutants,
criteria pollutant nonattainment areas, and potential project-related impacts on air quality,
including temporary, long-term, and visibility effects in Class I Federal Areas (40 CFR Part 81,
Subpart D). EPA recommends that the environmental document quantify emissions of criteria and
hazardous air pollutants from project-related activities; specify emission sources (mobile,
stationary, fugitive, area, and ground disturbance); and evaluate appropriate mitigation measures.
EPA further recommends inclusion of a Construction Emissions Mitigation Plan, incorporating
relevant requirements to minimize particulate matter and toxic air emissions. The environmental
document should identify applicable air permits, such as New Source Review and Title V, for the
proposed action.

Northern’s Response:

Northern’s Resource Report 9, Section 9.1.1.3 provides a discussion of ambient air conditions
and Section 9.1.1.2 provides a discussion of National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS)
and non-NAAQS pollutants, as well as criteria pollutant nonattainment areas. Section 9.1.3 and
9.1.4 identify potential project impacts on air quality including emissions, emission sources,
potential mitigation and construction emissions. Section 9.1.2.1 discusses New Source Review
permitting and Title V operating permits are discussed in Section 9.1.2.3.
                                                                                     Attachment A


EPA’s Comment:

Hazardous Materials, Hazardous Waste, and Solid Waste

EPA recommends the environmental document evaluate impacts from solid, hazardous, and
other waste generated by the proposed action in accordance with RCRA Subtitle C and D,
TSCA, and other applicable regulations. The environmental document should identify waste
types, volumes, and management plans; address applicable federal requirements; and evaluate
mitigation measures, including waste minimization and use of less toxic alternatives.

EPA also recommends assessing risks from hazardous waste transport, including potential
accidental releases, and identifying any contaminated sites that may be encountered during
project-related activities and how they will be managed.

Northern’s Response:

Northern’s Resource Report 2, Section 2.2.4.1 provides a discussion of potential impacts from
project waste and Section 2.1.4 discusses potential sources of groundwater contamination,
including mitigation measures to prevent potential incidental releases, and Table 2.1.4-1 lists
known potential sources of contamination, including mapped Resource Conservation and
Recovery Act locations. Northern will adhere to state and federal permit conditions related to use,
transportation, and clean up of potential hazardous wastes such as fuel and horizontal directional
drill additives.
                                                                                         Attachment A


EPA’s Comment:

National Historic Preservation Act and Executive Order 13007

EPA recommends the environmental document address compliance with Section 106 of the
National Historic Preservation Act or other applicable state law. The environmental document
should address the presence of cultural and historic resources and their eligibility for listing on the
National Register, including Indian sacred sites and traditional cultural properties, and describe
how the lead agency will avoid adverse effects to resources. EPA further recommends
summarizing all coordination and consultation with State Historic Preservation Officer
(SHPO)/Tribal Historic Preservation Officer, Tribes, and other parties.

Northern’s Response:

Northern’s Resource Report 4 addresses cultural resources potentially impacted by the Project.
Section 4.1 provides a discussion of Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act and
Sections 4.4 and 4.5 provide a summary of coordination/consultation with the State Historic
Preservation Offices and Native American Tribes. Section 4.3.2 clarifies that no cultural and/or
historic resources will be impacted by the Project.

Data Request 6 (Resource Report 1 – General Project Description):
Identify any non-jurisdictional facilities associated with the project, including auxiliary facilities built by
other companies and any facilities proposed by customers. As applicable, provide the following
information for each facility:
    a) a brief description of each facility, including its owner or sponsor;
    b) the county and state;
    c) gas consumption or megawatt size, as appropriate;
    d) the length and diameter of any interconnecting pipeline or power line to be constructed;
    e) land requirements;
    f) required permits, including any applicable regulatory siting process;
    g) the latest status of federal, state, and local permits/approvals, including consultations with the
        State Historic Preservation Office, FWS, and NMFS;
    h) the current status and schedule of the project; and
    i) current 1:24,000/1:25,000 scale topographic maps showing the location of the facilities relative to
        the proposed jurisdictional facilities.

Response:
The non-jurisdictional facilities identified in Resource Report 1, Section 1.10 are for the proposed Hobbs
compressor station. The Hobbs compressor station will require new commercial electric power lines to
provide electric service from a local provider, new communications line, water and septic system.
Northern has requested electrical service from a local utility company for the Hobbs compressor station.
The local utility company will provide the necessary equipment and perform the construction activities.
Northern is planning redundant communications, which would include fiber optic and/or landline for the
compressor station communications. Communication equipment and construction activities will be
provided by local communication company. Northern is working with the local communication company
on the location of the communication line.
Northern plans to install a water well and septic system including tank and leach field within the proposed
Hobbs compressor station property. The water and septic facilities will be less than 0.1 acre in size and
located in the operational footprint that was included in the Section 7(c) application. Northern will obtain
the necessary local permits to complete well and septic system installations.
These non-jurisdictional facilities will not have impacts on wetlands or sensitive wildlife habitats. All
contracted utility companies will obtain the necessary environmental construction permits.

INTRODUCTION

This Unanticipated Discovery Plan outlines procedures to be followed by Northern Natural Gas (Northern)
in the event of an unanticipated discovery of archaeological resources or human remains during
construction associated with the Permian Basin Expansion Project in the State of New Mexico. Northern
contractors, where applicable, shall also follow the procedures outlined in this plan. The procedures differ
depending on whether potentially significant cultural materials (Section I) or human remains (Section II)
are encountered.

I.       Unanticipated Discovery of Archaeological Resources

     1. When previously unidentified archaeological resources are discovered during ground disturbing
        activities within the project construction area, work will stop immediately to protect the integrity
        of the discovery, and Northern’s on-site Environmental Inspector will be notified of the discovery.

     2. Immediately following notification of the discovery, the Environmental Inspector will:

         i)      Inspect the work site to determine the extent of the discovery. No cultural material will
                 be removed from its original location;
         ii)     Halt all construction work within 50 feet of the discovery and in the surrounding area
                 where further subsurface remains can reasonably be expected to occur;
         iii)    Clearly mark the area of the discovery using flagging and fencing, and protect it from the
                 elements if necessary; and
         iv)     Notify Northern’s Environmental Compliance Manager. If the discovery is on public land,
                 Northern’s Environmental Compliance Manager will notify the land management agency.

                 Environmental Compliance Manager: Terry Plucker
                 Phone Number:                     Office (402) 398-7226; Mobile (402) 332-7081
                 E-Mail:                           terry.plucker@nngco.com

     3. Northern’s Environmental Compliance Manager will direct an archaeological consultant to the
        project area to determine if the discovery consists of potentially significant materials. All actions
        involving the identification, evaluation, treatment, and reporting of historic properties, as defined
        by the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards and Guidelines for Archaeology and Historic
        Preservation (48 FR 44716, since amended), shall be carried out under the direct supervision of a
        person(s) meeting the Secretary of the Interior’s Professional Qualifications Standards for
        archaeology, architectural history, or history, as appropriate (36 CFR Part 61) and familiar with
        implementation of the New Mexico Cultural Properties Act (NM Stat. §§ 18-6-1 through 18-6-17).

II.       Unanticipated Discovery of Human Remains

When unmarked human burials or suspected human skeletal remains are encountered during
construction activities, Northern and contractors shall comply with the New Mexico Cultural Properties
Act—Human Burials in Unmarked Burial Grounds (NM Stat. § 18-6-11.2). The following steps are to be
taken any time human remains are unearthed, or other artifacts associated with mortuary features are
found during project construction or maintenance activities in New Mexico.

      1. Upon discovery of suspected human remains during construction, including bone or other
         remains suspected to be human, work shall immediately cease in the area. The construction
         contractor or utility inspector will immediately notify Northern’s Environmental Inspector. If there
         is uncertainty as to whether remains are human or of faunal origin, the New Mexico SA shall be
         contacted to make the determination.

migratory birds published by the USFWS in 2024. Northern does not intend to implement measures that
are not applicable to pipeline construction. The applicable measures Northern will implement are listed
below.

General Measures

   •   Northern will not collect birds, their parts, or nests.
   •   Northern will ensure that enclosed solid waste receptacles are available across Project work areas.
       All solid wastes generated will be containerized and properly disposed of offsite in compliance
       with applicable state and/or local waste disposal regulations.
   •   Northern will notify the local USFWS ESFO if it suspects that birds were illegally killed or if five
       or more birds are found dead during construction of the Project.
Habitat Protection
   •   Northern will survey and stake all workspaces to mark the limits of construction, vegetation
       clearing, grading, access roads, and pipeline or aboveground facility installation.
   •   Northern has designed the Project to minimize impacts on migratory birds by routing the pipeline
       and siting aboveground facilities within or adjacent to previously disturbed lands, including active
       agricultural fields, oil and gas well pads, access roads, and utility rights-of-way.
   •   Northern confirmed that the Project is not within an area designated as an Important Bird Area.
   •   Temporary erosion control devices will be removed following successful stabilization of
       workspaces.
Vegetation Removal
   •   Northern will conduct routine vegetation maintenance of the full width of the permanent pipeline
       easement outside of the primary migratory bird nesting season (April 15 – August 1) in accordance
       with the FERC Plan.

This Unanticipated Discovery Plan outlines procedures to be followed by Northern Natural Gas (Northern)

contractors, where applicable, shall also follow the procedures outlined in this plan. The procedures differ
depending on whether potentially significant cultural materials (Section I) or human remains (Section II)
are encountered.

I.       Unanticipated Discovery of Archaeological Resources

     1. When previously unidentified archaeological resources are discovered during ground disturbing
        activities within the project construction area, work will stop immediately to protect the integrity
        of the discovery, and Northern’s on‐site Environmental Inspector will be notified of the discovery.

     2. Immediately following notification of the discovery, the Environmental Inspector will:

         i)      Inspect the work site to determine the extent of the discovery. No cultural material will
                 be removed from its original location;
         ii)     Halt all construction work within 50 feet of the discovery and in the surrounding area
                 where further subsurface remains can reasonably be expected to occur;
         iii)    Clearly mark the area of the discovery using flagging and fencing, and protect it from the
                 elements if necessary; and
         iv)     Notify Northern’s Environmental Compliance Manager. If the discovery is on public land,
                 Northern’s Environmental Compliance Manager will notify the land management agency.

        Preservation (48 FR 44716, since amended), shall be carried out under the direct supervision of a
        person(s) meeting the Secretary of the Interior’s Professional Qualifications Standards for
        archaeology, architectural history, or history, as appropriate (36 CFR Part 61) and familiar with

Data Request 19 (Resource Report 5 – Socioeconomics):
Describe Northern’s outreach and consultation with local fire departments and emergency providers.

Response:
Every year Northern has a Public Awareness and Damage Prevention Program that calls for communication
with emergency responders. Communication revolves around pipeline safety: how to identify a pipeline
marker, what a pipeline right-of-way is and looks like, who to call in case of an emergency, physical
properties of natural gas and what is expected of first responders during an emergency.

Northern employs an emergency management response team to respond to pipeline leaks and other
emergencies. Team members conduct regular mock and table-top drills. In the event of a leak or emergency,
a “call burst” is sent to team members. Response to the situation is conducted using a command-and-control
system and is directed from a state-of-the-art command center in Northern’s Omaha, Nebraska, headquarters
building. Northern has established an alternate command center at a secondary location away from
Northern’s headquarters, if needed.

Northern has developed emergency response plans for its entire system. Operating personnel attend training
for emergency response procedures and plans, pursuant to Occupational Safety and Health Administration’s
regulations in 29 CFR Part 1910. Northern will review, revise and develop new emergency response plans
as necessary before placing the new facilities in operation. Northern operations staff will meet with Local
Emergency Planning Committees (LEPC), including fire departments and police departments, to review
their plans. Northern will work with these LEPCs to communicate the specifics about the pipeline facilities
in the area and the need for emergency response. Northern also will meet periodically with these entities to
review and revise their plans when necessary. LEPC personnel will be involved in any operator-simulated
emergency exercises and post-exercise critiques, if conducted. Northern will use all available, reasonable
and relevant means to support the pipeline and facilities if an emergency occurs.

No special fire-fighting apparatus is required to fight a high-pressure natural gas fire at the proposed
facilities. The most effective and immediate way to begin to address a high-pressure gas pipeline rupture is
to shut off the gas source. Northern has valves spaced along the pipeline that can be used to isolate each
pipeline segment. Any gas remaining in the pipe segment is then allowed to burn off.

Data Request 25 (Resource Report 7 – Soils):
Confirm that shallow petrocalcic soils would be encountered during construction and discuss how
Northern would handle these materials. Also, describe any measures Northern would implement to avoid,
reduce, or mitigate effects associated with these materials.

Response:
Petrocalcic soils (i.e., soils with a shallow, cemented layer) are expected to be encountered along the pipeline
route. Petrocalcic horizons may have a hardened platy caliche, or hardpan soil layer cemented by calcium
carbonate. If a shallow petrocalcic horizon is encountered during trenching activities, Northern will use deep
tilling, ripping, rock hammering, or similar methods to break up the hardpan layer. Blasting is not anticipated
to construct in petrocalcic soils. Excavated petrocalcic horizons will be considered rock debris and not be
used to pad the pipe or left on the surface.

Decompaction outside of the trench line will be completed to the amount and depth necessary to achieve a
level of compaction relief similar to immediately off right of way.
